findings.title: Cleanup logs full ID batches at Error level
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error on every batch for both the ID fetch and the delete (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including the full ids slice and the SQL condition. These run on the success path (err is nil) and again when a batch finds nothing. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize in the thousands, each line can dump tens of thousands of IDs. That floods production logs, trips error-based alerts, and allocates large log payloads on every cleanup cycle. These should be removed or dropped to debug without the ID list before merge.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: Run now uses time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1) instead of 10 minutes. The PR is only about splitting annotation cleanup queries to avoid MySQL deadlocks; nothing in the description changes the job cadence. clean() still uses a 9-minute timeout that was sized for a 10-minute period, so a slow cycle now finishes and immediately starts another. Annotation cleanup is exactly the workload that was deadlocking writers, so running it about 10x more often increases DB load and makes that failure mode more likely. Restore the 10-minute interval unless the schedule change is intentional and the timeout is updated to match.

findings.title: SQLite ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation
findings.body: When the dialect is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs builds the IN-list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) once per ID. Each iteration copies the entire growing string. The new test uses batch size 32767, so this path copies on the order of hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes of intermediate strings per DELETE and can stall or time out cleanup (and CI) for a batch that was supposed to be a simple workaround for SQLite's parameter limit. Build the list with strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.
